intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. The note under each slide explains it, gives you something to remember and warns where people slip. Work each worked example in pencil before reading the answer, then close the page and try the recall questions.

sections.title: What counts as urban
sections.big_idea: India counts a place as urban in two ways. A **statutory town** has a municipality, and a **census town** only passes tests while a gram panchayat still governs it.
in_plain_words: A state notification makes a statutory town. It brings an elected urban body, a municipal budget and property tax. A census town is a statistical category: a place with at least 5,000 people, at least 75 per cent of male main workers outside agriculture and a density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre, all three together.

The edges matter as much. An outgrowth is a village-like area beside a statutory town that has urban features but sits outside its limits. An urban agglomeration adds a town and its outgrowths for counting, and **no single council governs it**. Census towns multiplied from 1,362 to 3,894 between 2001 and 2011.

diagram.caption: two ways to be urban, and two units at the edge

key_terms.meaning: A place a state law defines as urban, with a municipality or similar body.
A place with no municipal status that passes all three Census tests.
A village with urban features beside a statutory town, outside its limits.
A town and its outgrowths, or contiguous towns, counted as one unit.
A village moving into an urban category, often with a change of schemes.

worked_example.title: Sort three places
worked_example.setup: Invented places. A has a notified municipal corporation. B has no municipality, 6,000 people, 80 per cent of male main workers off-farm and 500 persons per sq km. C has 20,000 people, no municipality, 300 per sq km.
steps: A was notified under state municipal law, so it is a statutory town.
B has no municipality, so check the three census-town tests, all of which must pass.
B passes size (6,000 against 5,000), workforce (80 against 75) and density (500 against 400).
C passes size easily but fails the density test of 400, so the Census keeps it rural.
worked_example.answer: A is a statutory town, B is a census town and C stays rural, whatever its size.

mistakes: Treating a census town as a town with a municipality. The Census counts its people as urban while the state governs it as a village.
Quoting a count of towns without saying the year and the list it comes from.
Assuming a large village is urban. It stays rural unless it passes all three tests at once.

recall.q: What are the three census-town tests?
recall.a: At least 5,000 people, at least 75 per cent of male main workers outside agriculture, and a density of at least 400 persons per square kilometre.

recall.q: How many census towns did Census 2011 identify, against 2001?
What is an outgrowth?
recall.a: A village or hamlet with urban features, touching a statutory town but outside its legal limits.

recall.q: Which Census 2027 item fixes town boundaries?
recall.a: Administrative units were frozen as on 1 January 2026.

recall.q: Who pushed for municipal status in the census-town study?
recall.a: Mostly local elites and traders. Poorer groups resisted, fearing the loss of rural welfare schemes.

sections.title: How fast and where India urbanises
sections.big_idea: India's urban share climbs slowly, about **0.3 points a year**, and the largest urban populations sit in states with modest urban shares.
in_plain_words: The World Bank series rises from 17.9 per cent in 1960 to 35.7 per cent in 2025. Census 2011 counted 37.7 crore urban residents, 31.2 per cent of the population. It was the first decade in which towns added more people than villages.

A national average hides the states. Urban shares in 2011 ran from about 10 per cent to 97 per cent. Uttar Pradesh was under a quarter urban yet second in urban residents. **Read a share beside the headcount**, and check which definition and year stand behind any urban figure.

diagram.caption: the same four states ranked two ways

key_terms.meaning: Urban population as a percentage of the total population.
A city of 10 lakh people or more.
The High Powered Expert Committee on urban infrastructure, chaired by Isher Judge Ahluwalia.
A what-if calculation, such as counting villages over 10,000 people as urban.
The Periodic Labour Force Survey, the source of the work figures.

worked_example.title: Check the 2011 urban share
worked_example.setup: Census 2011 counted about 37.71 crore urban residents and 83.35 crore rural residents.
steps: Total population: 37.71 + 83.35 = 121.06 crore.
The slide gives 31.2 per cent for 2011, so the counts agree with the share.
worked_example.answer: Urban share is 31.2 per cent, which matches the deck.

mistakes: Comparing India's urban share with another country's without noting that each country defines urban differently.
Reading a state's urban share as its urban headcount. Uttar Pradesh shows how far apart they can be.
Treating post-2011 shares as counted figures. They are projections until Census 2027.

recall.q: By roughly how much does the urban share rise each year?
recall.a: About 0.3 points a year over six decades.

recall.q: What did the HPEC counterfactual show?
recall.a: If villages above 10,000 people counted as urban, India would have been over 35 per cent urban in 2010, instead of about 30.

recall.q: Which large state was under a quarter urban in 2011 yet second in urban residents?
recall.a: Uttar Pradesh, at 22.3 per cent and 4.45 crore.

recall.q: What share of urban women were in the labour force in 2025?
recall.a: 27.7 per cent, against 45.9 per cent of rural women.

recall.q: Why does a grant based on urban population favour Uttar Pradesh?
recall.a: Its urban headcount is large, though its councils are among the weakest.

sections.title: The 74th Amendment and the Twelfth Schedule
sections.big_idea: The 74th Amendment fixed that municipalities **exist and are elected**, and left their powers, taxes and money to each state.
in_plain_words: Part IXA of the Constitution, Articles 243P to 243ZG, requires elected municipalities with a five-year term, a State Election Commission, reserved seats, a State Finance Commission and planning committees. The Twelfth Schedule lists eighteen functions, from planning and roads to burials and slaughter houses.

Then comes the catch. Article 243W says a state legislature **may** endow municipalities with powers, so devolution is optional. The CAG found on average only 4 of 18 functions fully under autonomous control, and many states had not formed the planning committees at all.

diagram.caption: each layer sets what the layer below may do

key_terms.meaning: The part of the Constitution on municipalities, Articles 243P to 243ZG.
The list of eighteen functions a state may give to municipalities.
Lets states decide how much of the Schedule to devolve.
Runs municipal elections and holds the rolls under Article 243ZA.
A district or metropolitan body that joins local plans (243ZD, 243ZE).

worked_example.title: Which Article answers it?
worked_example.setup: A reader asks four questions about one municipality. Match each to the Article that governs it.
steps: How long can the council sit before a fresh election? Article 243U, five years.
Who decides which taxes it may levy? Article 243X, through state law.
Who runs its election? Article 243ZA, the State Election Commission.
Must it have a wards committee? Article 243S, if it has 3 lakh people or more.

mistakes: Reading the Twelfth Schedule as a list of what every municipality does. Article 243W only permits states to devolve it.
Assuming the Election Commission of India runs municipal polls. The State Election Commission does.
Expecting planning committees to exist. The audit found few had been formed or had prepared plans.

recall.q: How many functions are in the Twelfth Schedule?
recall.a: Eighteen.

recall.q: What is the term of a municipality, and how soon must a new election follow a dissolution?
recall.a: Five years, and a fresh election must be completed within six months of a dissolution.

recall.q: What does Article 243W say a state may do?
recall.a: Endow municipalities by law with the powers needed to function as institutions of self-government.

recall.q: What fraction of seats must be reserved for women?
recall.a: Not less than one-third of all directly elected seats, counting the SC and ST women's seats.

recall.q: What did the CAG find about District Planning Committees?
recall.a: Only 10 of 18 audited states had constituted them, and only 3 had prepared annual district plans.

sections.title: Who runs a town, from councils to staff
sections.big_idea: A municipality has several offices filled in different ways, and **the person who signs is often chosen by the state**.
in_plain_words: Councillors are elected from wards. The mayor is chosen by state law, directly in a few states and by the council elsewhere. The commissioner is appointed by the state and runs staff, contracts and the budget. In Delhi and Mumbai executive power sits with the commissioner, and in Kolkata with a mayor-in-council.

The picture is weaker than the law suggests. The CAG found 61 per cent of 2,625 audited bodies with no elected council, one sanctioned post in three vacant, and parastatals doing municipal work. Bengaluru shows the pattern: **a state-led authority above several corporations**.

diagram.caption: four offices, four ways of being filled

key_terms.meaning: The state-appointed executive head of a municipality.
A model where the mayor and elected members hold executive power.
A post the state has approved for a municipality.
A development authority, water board or similar agency doing municipal work.
A special purpose vehicle, such as those the Smart Cities Mission created.

worked_example.title: Size the problem
worked_example.setup: Illustrative use of the audit figures. The audit covered 2,625 bodies, 61 per cent without an elected council. A town has 300 sanctioned posts and one in three is vacant.
steps: Bodies without a council: 2,625 × 61 ÷ 100 = 1,601.
The slide rounds this to about 1,600.
Vacancies in the illustrative town: 300 ÷ 3 = 100.
Those 100 empty posts sit on top of any shortage in the sanctioned number itself.
worked_example.answer: About 1,600 bodies had no council, and the illustrative town has 100 vacant posts.

mistakes: Lobbying councillors in a commissioner city without finding out who the commissioner's office will act on.
Measuring staffing against vacancies only. If the state sanctions too few posts, a full roll still leaves work undone.
Assuming the municipality runs every service in town. Parastatals and SPVs often hold the function.

recall.q: How is the commissioner appointed?
recall.a: By the state government.

recall.q: Which cities use a commissioner system?
recall.a: Delhi and Mumbai.

recall.q: What did the CAG find about elected councils?
recall.a: 61 per cent of 2,625 urban local bodies in 17 states had none.

recall.q: What does a vacancy rate measure?
recall.a: Empty posts against sanctioned posts.

recall.q: What did Bengaluru's 2024 law create?
recall.a: A Greater Bengaluru Authority chaired by the Chief Minister, with up to seven corporations.

sections.title: Municipal finance
sections.big_idea: Municipal corporations raise about **0.6 per cent of GDP**, and much of their own money comes from property tax that is badly collected.
in_plain_words: In 2023-24 the 232 corporations budgeted ₹1,70,722 crore of revenue, 0.6 per cent of GDP. Own revenue was 61.9 per cent of it, state transfers 28.7 per cent and central transfers 2.5 per cent. Property tax was 19.0 per cent of revenue and over 60 per cent of own tax revenue.

Three state decisions set a body's own revenue: which taxes it may levy, who sets the rates and who collects. Without audited accounts there is no grant and no bond, and **budget estimates are not actual spending**. Always ask for both.

key_terms.meaning: Money a body receives for running costs, from taxes, fees and transfers.
Tax and non-tax income a municipality raises itself.
The main municipal tax, set and assessed under state law.
Water produced but not billed. AMRUT 2.0 sets a target of under 20 per cent.
A planned figure, which may differ from the actual spent.

worked_example.title: Read the revenue mix
worked_example.setup: Use the 2023-24 budget figures for 232 corporations.
steps: Own revenue 61.9 per cent and transfers 31.2 per cent leave the remainder: 100 − 61.9 − 31.2 = 6.9%.
State and central transfers add up to 28.7 + 2.5 = 31.2%, the transfers share used above.
Property tax: 1,70,722 × 19 ÷ 100 = 32,437 crore.
worked_example.answer: Other receipts are 6.9 per cent, and property tax is about ₹32,437 crore.

mistakes: Reading a high own-revenue share as strength. It can also mean small transfers.
Using corporation figures for all municipalities. The RBI reports cover only corporations.
Quoting a budget capital figure as spending that happened.

recall.q: What share of GDP do municipal corporations raise?
recall.a: About 0.6 per cent in 2023-24.

recall.q: What are the four causes of weak property tax listed?
recall.a: Undervaluation, incomplete property lists, policy gaps and weak administration and collection.

recall.q: Which entry condition ties accounts to grants?
recall.a: Publishing provisional and audited accounts, required by the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions.

recall.q: How much more did state transfers contribute than central ones?
recall.a: State transfers were 28.7 per cent of receipts against 2.5 per cent from the Centre.

recall.q: What does Bengaluru's self-assessment scheme show?
recall.a: A simple method raised yield 33 per cent in 2001 and kept compliance costs down.

sections.title: Transfers, Finance Commissions and borrowing
sections.big_idea: Union grants to cities nearly triple in the 16th award, but **conditions matter more than the cash**, and bonds stay tiny.
in_plain_words: The 15th Finance Commission gave ₹1,21,055 crore to urban local bodies for 2021-26. The 16th gives ₹3,56,257 crore for 2026-31, split into a basic grant, a performance grant, a special infrastructure component and a one-time urbanisation premium. Every grant needs elected bodies, published accounts and a timely State Finance Commission.

Borrowing is thin. Municipal bonds stood at ₹4,204 crore in March 2024, 0.01 per cent of GDP, while Pune's 2017 bond pledged property tax and carried AA+ ratings. Challenge funds now reward cities that can prepare bankable projects, and **small towns find that hardest**.

key_terms.meaning: A rule a state or body must meet before it gets any local body grant.
A one-time ₹10,000 crore reward for merging peri-urban villages into towns.
The body that recommends how state taxes are shared with municipalities.
A bond repaid from a named income, such as Pune's pledged property tax.
A fund that pays for projects cities win by meeting conditions.

worked_example.title: Check the 16th award
worked_example.setup: The four urban grants of the 16th Finance Commission, in crore rupees, are 2,32,125, 58,032, 56,100 and 10,000. Rural local bodies get 4,35,236.
steps: Total for rural and urban: 3,56,257 + 4,35,236 = 7,91,493.
worked_example.answer: The urban grants total ₹3,56,257 crore, about 45 per cent of the rural and urban total.

mistakes: Judging a grant by its size. The entry conditions decide who gets it.
Counting a State Finance Commission that was constituted and then ignored as proof of reform.
Telling a small town to compete for a challenge fund without checking it has accounts, a rating and project staff.

recall.q: What are the three entry conditions in the 16th award?
recall.a: Local bodies constituted as the Constitution requires, provisional and audited accounts published, and the State Finance Commission constituted on time.

recall.q: How much did the 15th Commission allocate to urban local bodies?
What did the Pune bond pledge?
recall.a: Property tax, for a ₹200 crore, ten-year issue rated AA+.

recall.q: What is the Urban Challenge Fund condition on private money?
recall.a: At least 50 per cent of project cost must come from bonds, bank loans and public-private partnerships.

recall.q: Why is the HPEC maintenance estimate relevant?
recall.a: It puts upkeep at ₹19.9 lakh crore, roughly half its capital estimate, which new assets hand to the municipality.

sections.title: The urban missions
sections.big_idea: Five Union schemes shape a town in 2026, and each has its **own money, target and status**, which change with time.
in_plain_words: AMRUT 2.0 aims at a tap in every statutory town and was extended to March 2027. The Smart Cities Mission closed on 31 March 2025 with 7,741 of 8,064 projects complete. PMAY-Urban 2.0 offers four routes to a house, and SBM-Urban 2.0 covers waste and used water. PM SVANidhi lends to street vendors.

Delivery lags the announcements. Of ₹66,060 crore committed for AMRUT 2.0 sewerage, 34 per cent had been released. Completed houses exceed occupied ones. **Each mission also leaves running costs** for the municipality once the Union money ends, so ask who pays after closure.

diagram.caption: five schemes, one municipality to run them

key_terms.meaning: The urban water mission aiming at a tap in every statutory town.
An area-based programme run through city SPVs, financially closed in March 2025.
Housing scheme with BLC, AHP, ARH and interest subsidy verticals.
A sanitation status SBM-U 2.0 targets for all statutory towns.
A Union scheme of bank loans for street vendors.

worked_example.title: Test two progress claims
worked_example.setup: Use the Smart Cities and AMRUT figures on the slides.
steps: Smart Cities projects: 7,741 complete + 323 ongoing = 8,064.
Completion rate: 7,741 ÷ 8,064 = 96%.
AMRUT 2.0 sewerage money released: 22,763 ÷ 66,060 = 34%.
Read both: projects were mostly built, but only 18 cities finished all of theirs.
worked_example.answer: Smart Cities finished about 96 per cent of projects, while AMRUT sewerage released 34 per cent of the money.

mistakes: Assuming a scheme is still running because it was announced. Check the Ministry for the current status.
Treating a ministry achievement figure as independent evidence.
Forgetting the running cost of command centres, cameras and treatment plants after a mission closes.

recall.q: When did the Smart Cities Mission reach financial closure?
recall.a: 31 March 2025.

recall.q: What is AMRUT 2.0's tap target?
recall.a: 2.68 crore tap connections.

recall.q: What are the four PMAY-U 2.0 verticals?
recall.a: Beneficiary-Led Construction, Affordable Housing in Partnership, Affordable Rental Housing and Interest Subsidy Scheme.

recall.q: What are the income limits for EWS, LIG and MIG?
recall.a: EWS up to ₹3 lakh, LIG ₹3 to 6 lakh, MIG ₹6 to 9 lakh a year.

recall.q: Why does the Ministry report completed and occupied houses separately?
recall.a: A finished house is not always lived in.

sections.title: Slums, housing and street vendors
sections.big_idea: A better house does not guarantee a better life, and the **tenure, networks and legal rights** around it decide the outcome.
in_plain_words: PMAY-U 2.0 defines a slum by size and conditions only: at least 300 people or about 60 to 70 households in poor tenements. Tenable slums can be redeveloped where they stand, and untenable ones may be resettled. Upgrading, in-situ redevelopment, resettlement and rental housing each carry a different risk.

A 14-year lottery study found relocated winners gained better houses but no gain in income, tenure security or human capital, and 34 per cent never moved in. Street vendors have a legal route instead. The Street Vendors Act, 2014 **protects them only after the town survey is done** and certificates are issued.

diagram.caption: where the household ends up after the scheme

key_terms.meaning: A slum that can be redeveloped where it stands.
Replacing a low-rise settlement with flats on the same land.
Proof a surveyed vendor aged 14 or more holds under the 2014 Act.
The body that surveys vendors, chaired by the commissioner.
A pattern where low income keeps people from using city opportunities.

worked_example.title: Size a vending zone
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A ward has 20,000 residents. Section 3(2) sets the norm for vending zones at two and a half per cent of the ward population.
steps: Take the norm: 2.5 per cent of the ward population.
Vendors to accommodate: 20,000 × 2.5 ÷ 100 = 500.
Before any eviction, the survey must be complete and certificates issued (section 3(3)).
If relocation is needed, thirty days' notice is required (section 18(3)).
worked_example.answer: The ward's vending zones should accommodate about 500 vendors.

mistakes: Counting only owners when listing households for a scheme. Renters, hostel residents and worksite workers are missed.
Treating a loan under PM SVANidhi as protection for the vendor's pitch.
Using 2001 slum shares as current figures. Switch to Census 2011 and then Census 2027 data.

recall.q: What size does the PMAY-U 2.0 definition set for a slum?
recall.a: At least 300 people, or about 60 to 70 households.

recall.q: Which PMAY-U 2.0 vertical covers rental housing?
recall.a: Affordable Rental Housing (ARH).

recall.q: What did the lottery study find after 14 years?
recall.a: Better housing but no change in tenure security, family income or human capital, and less informal insurance.

recall.q: What does section 3(3) of the Street Vendors Act bar?
recall.a: Eviction or relocation until the survey is complete and certificates are issued.

recall.q: Who must make up at least 40 per cent of a Town Vending Committee?
recall.a: Vendors elected by vendors, one-third of them women.

sections.title: Urban work and the job guarantee debate
sections.big_idea: Urban unemployment is highest among young women, and the case for an urban guarantee rests on **irregular work** more than on open unemployment.
in_plain_words: In 2025, 4.8 per cent of the urban labour force was unemployed, but 13.6 per cent of those aged 15 to 29 and 18.9 per cent of young urban women. Jean Drèze proposed DUET, in which public institutions hire registered workers through job stamps and the state pays wages directly. Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan have legislated their own versions.

Field evidence from Himachal Pradesh shows the limits: few bodies offered work, wages came late, and the budget fell from ₹100 crore to ₹5 crore. The rural guarantee also changed from 1 July 2026, which affects census towns. **Design choices decide whether the right is real**: who holds it, who provides work and how it is funded.

left.title: Himachal Pradesh scheme
items: 120 days a year at ₹300 a day
Outlay cut from ₹100 crore to ₹5 crore

right.title: Rajasthan Bill, 2023
items: Work within the ward or 5 km

diagram.caption: who holds the right, and for how many days

key_terms.meaning: Decentralised Urban Employment and Training, Jean Drèze's 2020 proposal.
A permit the state issues to a public institution to hire workers.
Payment if no work is offered within the stated days.
The 2025 rural guarantee law in force from 1 July 2026.
A measure of work activity used in PLFS estimates.

worked_example.title: What did 60 days mean?
worked_example.setup: Himachal Pradesh promises 120 days a year at ₹300 a day. Field workers mostly got fewer than 60 days.
steps: Promised earnings: 120 × 300 = 36,000 rupees a year.
Fewer than 60 days is under half the promise: 60 ÷ 120 = 50%.
At 60 days the pay would be 60 × 300 = 18,000 rupees, before any wage delay.
Late wages, one to two months, push the real value lower still.
worked_example.answer: A worker with 60 days gets at most half of the 36,000 rupees promised.

mistakes: Judging the need for a guarantee by the unemployment rate alone. It leaves out people outside the labour force and irregular work.
Assuming a village merged into a municipality keeps the rural guarantee. It leaves it.
Comparing household and individual entitlements as if they were the same right.

recall.q: What was the urban unemployment rate in 2025?
recall.a: 4.8 per cent, against 2.4 per cent in rural areas.

recall.q: How does DUET pay workers?
recall.a: The state pays the minimum wage straight to the worker's account.

recall.q: How many days does Himachal Pradesh promise?
recall.a: 120 days a year for every household.

recall.q: What does the VB-G RAM G Act apply to?
recall.a: Only rural areas that the Centre notifies.

recall.q: What share of urban workers is in proprietary and partnership enterprises?
recall.a: About two-thirds, 66 per cent.

sections.title: Heat, floods and the municipal role
sections.big_idea: Heat plans need coordination more than capital, but floods depend on **who controls water and land outside the municipality**.
in_plain_words: The IMD declares a heatwave when the maximum runs 5°C or more above normal for places with a normal below 40°C, 4°C or more above for hotter places, or above 45°C anywhere. After the May 2010 heatwave killed 1,344 more people than usual, Ahmedabad built India's first Heat Action Plan with outreach, early warning, training and cool roofs.

Floods split responsibility. Under 20 per cent of urban roads had storm water drains, and in Chennai in 2015 the CAG blamed a state department's reservoir releases and land use in the tank's foreshore. **Plan across agencies**, count the dead and damaged afterwards, and set thresholds from local data.

diagram.caption: the five-step chain, repeated each year

key_terms.meaning: A maximum 4 to 5°C above normal, or above 45°C anywhere.
Deaths above a reference level, here measured against a comparison period.
A roof treatment that keeps indoor temperatures 2 to 5°C lower.
A city plan with outreach, early warning, training and exposure cuts.
Land at the edge of a tank, whose use affected the Chennai discharge.

worked_example.title: Excess deaths and thresholds
worked_example.setup: Ahmedabad recorded 4,462 deaths in May 2010 against a reference of 3,118. For the IMD rule, take a station with a normal maximum of 38°C.
steps: Relative to the reference: 1,344 ÷ 3,118 = 43.1%.
The station's normal is below 40°C, so the threshold is the normal plus 5: 38 + 5 = 43 degrees.
Any maximum above 45°C also counts, whatever the normal.
worked_example.answer: 1,344 excess deaths, 43.1 per cent above reference, and a heatwave threshold of 43°C for that station.

mistakes: Relying on IMD thresholds alone. A city alert can use local health data.
Making a flood plan that stops at municipal limits, when reservoirs and land use sit with other agencies.
Planning for the season and skipping the review. The cycle ends by counting deaths and damage.

recall.q: How many excess deaths did the May 2010 Ahmedabad heatwave cause?
recall.a: 1,344, or 43.1 per cent above the reference.

recall.q: What are the four strategies of the Heat Action Plan?
recall.a: Public awareness, early warning, training of health staff, and reducing exposure including cool roofs.

recall.q: What share of urban roads had storm water drains?
recall.a: Under 20 per cent.

recall.q: What did the CAG find about the Chembarambakkam tank rules?
recall.a: They had not been revised for 23 years.

recall.q: Which Twelfth Schedule item underpins municipal climate work?
recall.a: Item 8, urban forestry and protection of the environment.

sections.title: Participation and what research has found
sections.big_idea: Residents reach a municipality through several channels, and **only elections are guaranteed**, so check the ward committee before you organise around it.
in_plain_words: Article 243S requires wards committees in municipalities of 3 lakh people or more. Area sabhas bring together all voters of a polling area where state law provides. The Town Vending Committee gives elected vendors at least 40 per cent of seats. Apps and surveys collect complaints and opinions but decide nothing.

The research tables gather the course's evidence: census towns, finance, the CAG audits, the Bengaluru law, the housing lottery, heat plans and job guarantees. The practice checklist turns it into questions about status, power, money and plans. **Every item has a public answer** if you ask for the document.

diagram.caption: channels ranked by legal weight, strongest first

key_terms.meaning: A committee for one or more wards, required at 3 lakh people (243S).
An assembly of all voters of a polling area, where state law provides.
A complaint channel, with over 2 crore resolved by 2021.
An annual ranking whose feedback is an input and decides nothing.
The original document behind a figure, such as a budget book.

worked_example.title: Seat a vending committee
worked_example.setup: Illustrative. A Town Vending Committee has 30 members. The Act asks at least 40 per cent vendors elected by vendors, one-third of them women, and at least 10 per cent from NGOs and community groups.
steps: Vendors: 30 × 40 ÷ 100 = 12 at least.
Women among those vendors: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 at least.
NGO and community members: 30 × 10 ÷ 100 = 3 at least.
The commissioner chairs the committee.
worked_example.answer: At least 12 vendors, of whom at least 4 are women, plus at least 3 NGO or community members.

mistakes: Organising residents around a ward plan without checking that the ward committee exists and has met.
Treating an app complaint count as evidence of participation in decisions.
Mixing findings from studies that cover different bodies, such as RBI corporations and CAG local bodies.

recall.q: Which Article requires wards committees, and at what size?
recall.a: Article 243S, in municipalities of 3 lakh people or more.

recall.q: Which participation channel is guaranteed by the Constitution?
recall.a: Ward elections.

recall.q: What happens to participation when a town is run by an administrator?
recall.a: Wards committees have no councillors to sit on them.

recall.q: Name two items from the practice checklist on money.
recall.a: Get the budget book and audited accounts, and find the property tax coverage and collection rate.

recall.q: What did the area sabhas do in Bengaluru before 2024?
recall.a: They proposed development priorities and identified scheme beneficiaries, until the select committee removed them.

notes.2: Use this agenda as a map of eleven sections. It runs from what counts as a town, to who governs it, to how it is paid for, to what it must deliver. Skim the slide ranges now so you know where to look when a question comes up later.
notes.4: Hold two labels in your head. A statutory town has a municipality because a state notified it. A census town only passes the Census tests and stays under a gram panchayat. Before asking how big a place is, ask who governs it.
notes.5: Treat the three census-town tests as three locks that must all open at once. A settlement of 20,000 people with low density stays rural. Read the right-hand column too: counting only male workers leaves women's non-farm work out of the test.
notes.6: Picture the edge of a city as rings. The statutory town is the core, the outgrowth hugs it, and the agglomeration adds them together for counting. The fastest growth sits outside the municipal plan, which is why Articles 243ZD and 243ZE ask for planning across the boundary.
notes.7: Read the three figures as one story. Census towns grew from 1,362 to 3,894, and a third of urban growth came from relabelling. Before you quote any urban count, ask which year, which list, and whether census towns sit inside it.
notes.8: The study found a busy small-town economy under village governance. Watch who asked for municipal status: local elites and traders pushed for it, and poorer groups feared losing rural welfare schemes. A change of status helps some residents and costs others, so ask who gains.
notes.9: Use this table as a before-and-after for a village that becomes a town. The rows to remember are the job guarantee, the housing scheme and the grants, because each switches to a different programme. Workers in Himachal Pradesh felt the change and gave the state's urban scheme a nickname.
notes.10: Treat Census 2027 as a calendar to work against. Phase 1 lists houses between April and September 2026, Phase 2 counts people in February 2027, and boundaries froze on 1 January 2026. The census town tests stay as in 2011, so urban figures for the two years compare directly.
notes.11: Read these questions as raw material for ward planning. Water source, latrine, rooms and ownership status become counts of households short of each service. Ask your state census office when ward-level tables will be released, and request ward maps that match the frozen boundaries.
notes.13: Read the line for its slope: about 0.3 points a year for six decades, from 17.9 to 35.7 per cent. It shows a steady climb with no sudden transition. Values after 2011 are projections, so treat them as estimates until Census 2027 reports.
notes.14: Memorise two numbers from 2011: 31.2 per cent urban and 37.7 crore urban residents. The decade also marks the first time towns added more people than villages. The projection of about 60 crore by 2031 depends on the present definition, so quote it with that condition.
notes.15: The national 31.2 per cent hides two different problems. In Tamil Nadu and Kerala the task is governing a continuous rural-urban belt. In Bihar and Uttar Pradesh it is weak small-town councils facing growth that has barely begun. Match your advice to the state type.
notes.16: Urban shares abroad rest on other definitions, so a gap between countries can come from the rulebook. India asks census towns to pass three tests together, which is demanding. The HPEC counterfactual makes the point: count villages above 10,000 people as urban and India passes 35 per cent in 2010.
notes.17: Notice the mismatch between share and size. Uttar Pradesh is under a quarter urban yet second in urban residents, so grants allocated by urban population flow in large amounts to states where councils are weakest. Always read a share beside the absolute number.
notes.18: Regular jobs cover half of urban workers, but regular does not mean secure. In 2023-24 over half had no written contract and nearly half had no social security. Remember too that two-thirds of urban workers sit in proprietary and partnership firms, which matters for any jobs scheme.
notes.19: Keep the gap in mind: 27.7 per cent of urban women are in the labour force against 45.9 per cent of rural women. The slide links it to transport, lighting, toilets and childcare, most of them municipal. Treat these services as employment services, since they shape who can take a job.
notes.20: This table teaches one habit: ask what each urban number counts. People, towns and local bodies are different units, and a projection differs from a complete count. When two figures disagree, check the unit, the year, and whether census towns are inside the count.
notes.22: Part IXA is where municipalities enter the Constitution. Learn the split. The Amendment fixed that councils exist, serve five years, are directly elected and have reserved seats and commissions. It left functions, taxes, the mayor and staff to state legislatures, and most later debates return to that split.
notes.23: Use this table as a reference and read the right-hand column closely. It lists what each Article leaves to the state, which is where real power sits. If you remember one pair, remember 243W for functions and 243X for money.
notes.24: Three labels, with no national thresholds. A town's type depends on how the Governor classifies it, so a corporation in one state may be smaller than a council in another. Check the state's law to learn which powers apply. The industrial township exception leaves some residents with no council to vote for.
notes.25: Learn the Twelfth Schedule in clusters: planning and land use (1 to 3), networks such as roads, water, sanitation and fire (4 to 7), environment (8), poverty and slums (9 to 11), and civic services (12 to 18). Item 8 later supports municipal climate work.
notes.26: The word to underline is 'may'. Article 243W permits states to hand over functions and does not require it. The audit found only 4 of 18 functions under autonomous control, which shows how little passes down. Before relying on a municipality, find out which agency in that town holds the function.
notes.27: Two rules to carry: councils serve five years, and an election must follow within six months of a dissolution. The State Election Commission runs the polls, and the Election Commission of India has no role. Delays often start earlier, when the state delimits wards and rotates reserved seats.
notes.28: These committees exist to join rural and urban plans, and the audit shows most do not work. Only 3 of 18 states had prepared annual district plans. If your project crosses a municipal edge, ask whether a planning committee exists and when it last met.
notes.29: Follow the four routes by which a municipality gets money: its own taxes, shares of state taxes, grants, and its funds. Article 243Y sends the sharing question to the State Finance Commission. Union Finance Commissions now use their own grants to push states to set one up.
notes.31: Four offices are filled in four ways. Councillors are elected from wards, the mayor depends on state law, and the commissioner is appointed by the state. The person who signs executive orders often answers to the state in practice. Find out which office acts before you lobby.
notes.32: Match the city to a model before you engage. In a commissioner city such as Delhi or Mumbai, executive power sits with an appointed officer, so a petition to councillors moves slowly. In Kolkata a mayor-in-council holds it. Map both offices, as the slide advises.
notes.33: Take the headline seriously: 61 per cent of 2,625 audited bodies had no elected council. The Constitution allows six months after a dissolution. The audit traces much of the delay to delimitation by state governments, and reform proposals move that task to State Election Commissions.
notes.34: Staffing is decided by the state, and the gaps are large. One sanctioned post in three is vacant, and the sanctioned list itself may be too short, as in Shimla. The definition of a sanctioned post shows why filling vacancies can still leave the work understaffed.
notes.35: Read Bengaluru as a case of redesign. One corporation became an authority chaired by the Chief Minister with up to seven corporations beneath it, and the area sabhas were dropped. Note the thresholds for a corporation: more than 10 lakh people and over ₹300 crore of local revenue.
notes.36: Each row is a test you can apply to any city law: who chairs the planning body, who can dissolve a council, which decisions need prior approval, and who sets property tax. Where the answer is the state, the power is only partly devolved.
notes.37: List every body that touches a service. Development authorities, water boards and SPVs often hold Twelfth Schedule functions and answer to state departments. Use the slide's test: for each service, write down who signs the contract, who collects the charge and who takes complaints. Expect three names.
notes.38: Reservation has layers, so work through them in order. SC and ST seats follow population share, one-third of those go to women, and one-third of all seats go to women. Rotation means a sitting councillor may lose the ward next term. Backward class reservation depends on the state.
notes.40: Anchor on 0.6 per cent of GDP, the revenue of 232 corporations in 2023-24. Compare it with 9.2 per cent collected by the Centre and 14.6 per cent by the states. These are the largest urban bodies, so smaller ones raise less. The capital figure comes from budgets, so read it as a plan.
notes.41: Own revenue is 61.9 per cent, but read it beside the total. A high share can mean strong taxes or tiny transfers. State transfers of 28.7 per cent dwarf the 2.5 per cent from the Centre, so the state shapes municipal budgets far more than the Centre does.
notes.42: Property tax is 19.0 per cent of corporation revenue and over 60 per cent of own tax revenue, yet at 0.09 to 0.11 per cent of GDP it sits far below OECD countries. Use the four causes as a checklist when diagnosing a weak town: valuation, property lists, policy and collection.
notes.43: Property tax reform is mostly about finding and valuing buildings. Bengaluru's self-assessment kept the method simple, and yield rose 33 per cent in 2001, with about a third of the rise from revaluation. Notice how the Finance Commissions now tie grants to floor rates and own-source growth.
notes.44: User charges raise the equity question the slide describes. Cost recovery lifts bills for households that already have a tap, while homes without a connection gain nothing until they are connected. That is why connections come first, and why lifeline tariffs for the first block of use are proposed.
notes.45: Two sets of numbers seem to clash. RBI shows corporations spending a high share on capital works, and the CAG shows most local bodies spending little on development. Both can be true, since they cover different bodies and RBI uses budget estimates. Remember the upkeep bill each new asset hands to the municipality.
notes.46: Accounts come before money. The 15th and 16th Finance Commissions require published provisional and audited accounts, and lenders need the same documents. Pune's bond shows the payoff. For your own research, collect budget books and audited accounts first, and ask for actual figures.
notes.47: Three state decisions govern a municipality's own revenue: which taxes it may levy, who sets the rates, and who collects. Compare Delhi, Kerala and Maharashtra, where corporations set their own property tax rates, with Bengaluru under the 2024 law. Use the table to judge how dependent a body is.
notes.48: Compare the two RBI reports to see what stayed constant: wider property tax coverage, better assessment, rule-based transfers and training. Both cover only municipal corporations, 201 in 2022 and 232 in 2024, so they say little about small towns.
notes.50: Remember the shape of the 15th award: ₹1,21,055 crore for urban local bodies, shared out by population and area, with entry conditions on published accounts and floor property tax rates. A further rule withheld all local body grants after March 2024 from states without a State Finance Commission.
notes.51: Read the 16th award by its conditions. Half of the basic grant is tied to sanitation, waste or water, and the performance grant rewards minimum growth in own revenue. The one-time urbanisation premium pays states that merge peri-urban villages into towns. Three entry conditions apply to every grant.
notes.52: Look at the jump: urban grants rise from ₹1,21,055 crore to ₹3,56,257 crore, and the urban share of the rural and urban total from about a third to about 45 per cent. The conditions matter more than the money, since they push states toward elections and published accounts.
notes.53: States hold the bigger lever. State transfers are more than ten times central transfers in corporation receipts, and they should follow a State Finance Commission. Use the five questions on the slide as an interview guide, and remember that a report tabled and ignored still meets the letter of the condition.
notes.54: Keep the scale in mind: ₹4,204 crore of bonds outstanding is 0.01 per cent of GDP. Pune's 2017 issue worked because property tax was pledged, the rating was AA+ and the accounts were audited. Banks and state agencies still lend more than the bond market does.
notes.55: Challenge funds reward readiness. A city must prepare a bankable project and raise at least half the money elsewhere, which takes audited accounts, a credit rating and staff who can write detailed project reports. Check whether a small town has that support before telling it to compete.
notes.56: Use this table to size the gap. Estimates range from ₹31 lakh crore for eight infrastructure sectors to ₹61.4 lakh crore over 2021 to 2036, and the maintenance estimate is about half the capital one. Check each estimate's period and price base before comparing it with any grant.
notes.58: Treat this table as a dashboard of five schemes, each with its own money, target and status. The statuses differ: Smart Cities has closed, AMRUT 2.0 was extended to March 2027, and SBM-U 2.0 was approved to 2025-26. Check the Ministry before assuming a scheme is live.
notes.59: AMRUT 2.0 aims at a tap in every urban household, with a target of 2.68 crore tap connections. Funds flow in three tranches against a State Water Action Plan built from city plans. Remember the reform conditions: recycled water for 20 per cent of demand and non-revenue water below 20 per cent.
notes.60: The Standing Committee found money moving slowly: ₹22,763 crore of ₹66,060 crore released, or 34 per cent. Keep the sanitation fact too: 68 per cent of surveyed septic tanks were not properly lined. Estimates of wastewater treated differ between NITI Aayog and the Ministry, so name your source.
notes.61: The mission closed with 7,741 of 8,064 projects complete, yet only 18 cities had finished every project. Read both numbers together: national completion is high, while few cities completed everything. When someone claims success, ask whether they count projects or cities.
notes.62: The mission leaves running costs behind. Command centres, cameras and software need staff and money now that the mission has closed. Use the four questions as a handover checklist, and read the listed causes of delay before blaming any single agency.
notes.63: Pick the vertical by the household's situation. Own land points to BLC, a purchase to AHP, renting to ARH, and a loan to the interest subsidy. Learn the income bands: EWS up to ₹3 lakh, LIG ₹3 to 6 lakh, MIG ₹6 to 9 lakh. Sharing is 60:40 for most states.
notes.64: Compare the three counts: sanctioned, completed and occupied. A finished house is not always lived in, which is why the Ministry reports occupation separately. Treat the gap between completed and occupied houses as a field question, and ask the households why they did not move in.
notes.65: SBM-U 2.0 shifts the focus from toilets to waste and used water. Learn the cost shares between Centre and state: the Centre pays more as cities get smaller, from 25 to 33 to 50 per cent. The achievements listed are the Ministry's own figures, and a ranking rewards only what it measures.
notes.66: A loan helps a vendor buy stock but gives no claim on a pitch. Protection comes from a survey and a certificate of vending under the 2014 Act. When working with vendors, ask both questions: did loans arrive, and has the town completed its survey and issued certificates?
notes.68: Be careful with the definition: 300 people or about 60 to 70 households in poor conditions. It says nothing about land ownership or length of stay, which state laws and town lists decide. Learn the split between tenable slums, redeveloped where they stand, and untenable ones, which may be resettled.
notes.69: These are 2001 figures, shown because they could be verified. Use them to see the range, from a fifth to over half of a city, and treat Patna's 0.3 per cent as a flag to check how settlements were listed. Switch to the Census 2011 slum tables for current work.
notes.70: Match each approach to its risk. Upgrading keeps people near work but may leave tenure open. Redevelopment hands upkeep costs to residents. Resettlement moves people away from jobs and schools, and rental housing may not fit short-stay workers. The order in which a town tries them decides who bears the cost.
notes.71: Read this as a lottery result, which makes winners and losers comparable. Fourteen years on, better houses came with no gain in income, tenure security or human capital, and with weaker family networks. Keep the 34 per cent who never took up the house in mind when judging take-up claims.
notes.72: The review argues that slums behave like a poverty trap, with human capital thresholds, investment inertia and a policy trap. The practice list is the useful part: extend services without waiting for title, ask what tenure a scheme confers, protect networks and count renters as well as owners.
notes.73: Work through the Act in order: survey (section 3(1)), accommodation in vending zones (3(2)), no eviction before the survey and certificates (3(3)), and thirty days' notice (18(3)). Section 22 sets the committee, with at least 40 per cent elected vendors.
notes.74: The survey is the gate to every protection. Until it is complete, vendors have no certificate to show an officer, so a town that never finishes it leaves the Act unused. The gaps PRS listed, such as no principles for zones or certificates, help explain why implementation stalls.
notes.75: Housing policy leans toward ownership, and three of the four PMAY-U 2.0 verticals help a household buy. The rental vertical serves workers and migrants. Census 2027 asks about ownership, rooms and married couples, so ward tables can show renting and crowding. A count that leaves out tenants undercounts need.
notes.77: Urban unemployment looks modest at 4.8 per cent, yet it reaches 13.6 per cent among 15 to 29 year olds and 18.9 per cent among young urban women. Remember what the rate leaves out: people not seeking work, and irregular low-paid work. That is why the guarantee case goes beyond open unemployment.
notes.78: Follow the four-step flow: the state issues job stamps, institutions hire registered workers, a placement agency assigns them, and the state pays wages straight to the worker's account. The design aim is to make public institutions the employers, which spreads the load beyond thin municipal staff.
notes.79: Compare the unit of entitlement first. Himachal Pradesh gives 120 days to a household, while Rajasthan's Bill gives at least 125 days to every adult. Then read the money signal: Himachal's outlay fell from ₹100 crore to ₹5 crore, which hollows out the promise.
notes.80: Field evidence shows a gap between paper and practice. Women were the majority of applicants, and nearly half of approved applications came from SC and ST workers. Yet few bodies offered work, most workers got fewer than 60 days, and none of those interviewed knew of the allowance.
notes.81: Read the table as a menu of design choices, remembering that the right-hand column is the course's own reading. An individual right gives women their own claim, many employers share the load, and late wages drive workers away. A state budget with no Union share can be cut in a single year.
notes.82: The rural guarantee changed on 1 July 2026: 125 workdays, a 60-day pause at sowing and harvest, and a 60:40 cost share. It applies only to rural areas the Centre notifies. Check whether census towns and merged villages are covered, since losing it may leave a resident with no scheme at all.
notes.83: Two-thirds of urban workers are in proprietary and partnership enterprises, so a guarantee paying the state minimum wage would compete with small firms for the same workers. Whether that lifts bottom wages or costs firms their workers is open. The schemes so far were too small to answer it.
notes.85: Learn the IMD rules in three lines: 5°C above normal where the normal is below 40°C, 4°C above where it is above 40°C, and any maximum above 45°C. Ahmedabad then set its own colour alerts. A city can set thresholds from local health data.
notes.86: The number to remember is 1,344 excess deaths, 43.1 per cent above the reference, with 4,462 deaths against 3,118. The counts came from municipal death records, so a routine municipal function supplied the evidence for heat planning.
notes.87: The plan has four strategies: outreach, early warning, training of health staff, and reduced exposure through cool roofs. Almost every action is municipal. The estimate of 2,380 deaths avoided in 2014 and 2015 comes from a comparison with a 2007 to 2010 baseline.
notes.88: Drains carry a quiet message: under 20 per cent of urban roads were covered by storm water drains. Flooding crosses boundaries, since tanks may belong to a state department and land use to a development authority. Ask who holds each piece before promising a flood fix.
notes.89: Study this as a case of decisions taken outside the municipality. A state department raised discharge from 12,000 to 20,960 cusecs to protect land in a tank's foreshore, and the operating rules were 23 years old. Flood plans that stop at municipal limits miss where risk is made.
notes.90: Use the five-step chain as a checklist: map exposure, set thresholds, name agencies, rehearse, and count afterwards. The heat and flood lists show which public documents to request. Start with the municipal death records and the list of reservoirs that drain through the town.
notes.91: This table sorts climate money by how much capital it needs. Heat plans need little and depend on coordination. Flood protection needs a lot and relies on control of land and water bodies. Notice that the 16th Finance Commission ties half its basic grant to sanitation, waste or water.
notes.93: Wards committees begin at 3 lakh people under Article 243S, and state law decides the rest. Area sabhas bring together every voter of a polling area. Bengaluru's 2024 law kept ward committees and dropped area sabhas, which were the most local channel of participation.
notes.94: Rank the channels by legal weight. Only elections are guaranteed by the Constitution, and only the first four channels have standing in decisions. Apps and surveys collect opinions that officials may ignore. Before organising a ward plan, check that the ward committee exists, when it last met and whether its minutes are public.
notes.95: Use this table as a one-page literature map for the first half of the course. Each row names a study and its main finding. Pick the row that fits your question and trace its source. The CAG and RBI studies cover different bodies, so keep their numbers apart.
notes.96: This table covers the second half. Two rows warn about interventions: a housing lottery gave better houses without higher income, and Himachal's urban guarantee saw its budget cut from ₹100 crore to ₹5 crore. The Ahmedabad row shows the estimated effect of a low-cost plan.
notes.97: Work this list as a first-week routine in a new town. The status questions come first because they decide who can act, and the money and evidence questions follow. Every item can be answered from a public document or a right to information request, so none needs a favour.
notes.98: Use this list to trace any figure in the course back to its source. When you quote a number in your own work, cite the original document, and read the closing line on the next slide about what the course left out.
notes.99: The second list ends with a statement of what was left out because no primary source could be opened: Census 2011 slum totals, detailed PM SVANidhi loan terms, and some CAG figures. Treat those as open gaps and find the primary document yourself before using them.
